draft.title: Using semicolons
card: A main clause is a group of words that makes complete sense on its own. It has a subject and a verb.
a semicolon can join two main clauses that are closely linked in meaning, with no conjunction. Example: The rain stopped; the oval was still a swamp.
a semicolon can separate items in a list when the items already contain commas. Example: We visited Perth, Western Australia; Hobart, Tasmania; and Darwin, Northern Territory.
Each part joined by a semicolon in the first use must be able to stand alone as a sentence. The semicolon shows the link between the ideas without a word such as and or but.
draft.remember: A semicolon links two related main clauses, or separates list items that already hold commas.

a.q: Which sentence uses a semicolon correctly?
opts: Mia trained all summer; she won the 800 metres
Mia trained all summer; and she won the 800 metres
Mia trained all summer; to win the 800 metres
Mia trained all summer; the 800 metres race
a.why: Both parts of the correct sentence are main clauses, and they are closely linked. The option with and keeps a conjunction, which the semicolon replaces. The others have a part that cannot stand alone.
a.clue: Check that both sides could be full sentences.

b.q: Which sentence uses semicolons to separate list items that already contain commas?
opts: We visited Cairns, Qld; Darwin, NT; and Perth, WA
We visited Cairns; Darwin; and Perth
We visited Cairns, Darwin, and Perth
We visited Cairns, Qld, Darwin, NT, and Perth, WA
b.why: Each item in the first sentence holds its own comma, so semicolons keep the three places clear. The second has plain items with no commas inside them. The third uses only commas, and the fourth runs the places together with commas.
b.clue: Look for items that have a comma inside them.

a.best: Mia trained all summer; she won the 800 metres

b.best: We visited Cairns, Qld; Darwin, NT; and Perth, WA

problems.detail: Why (b) says the fourth option 'runs the places together with commas', but the fourth option (We visited Cairns; Darwin; and Perth) uses semicolons, not commas. Its actual error is using semicolons between plain items that have no commas inside them. The explanation mixes up the third and fourth options and would confuse students.
